articles.title: Home Assistant brings Matter cameras into its camera views
articles.dek: Live video and snapshots use the existing interface, with a compatible Matter server required.
body: Home Assistant adds live video and snapshots for Matter 1.5 cameras through its existing camera interface. Artur Pragacz connects the camera support to the Matter server, while the video travels directly between the browser and camera.

The camera’s privacy settings determine whether it reports itself on, and active sessions determine its streaming state. Still images arrive as JPEG snapshots. Discovery requires a server with the camera interface introduced in schema 14.

This implements part of the first camera experience shaped in the public roadmap by Matthias Kerstner: using Home Assistant’s existing camera views. The new integration covers streams and snapshots, without establishing recording, two-way audio or full pan-and-tilt controls.

pullRequests.title: Support Matter cameras

externalSources.title: Support Matter cameras using the existing camera UI

articles.title: Home Assistant raises its browser minimums for older displays
articles.dek: iOS 12 devices and Fire tablets stuck on Chromium 59 fall below the new requirements.
body: Home Assistant raises its frontend minimums to Chrome 67, Safari and iOS 15.4, and Firefox 98. Browsers below those versions receive an explanation on the launch screen instead of remaining there indefinitely.

The change affects Apple devices that cannot move beyond iOS 12, including the first iPad Air and iPad mini 2 and 3. It also affects Fire tablets whose Amazon WebView remains on Chromium 59, including 2015 and 2016 models on Fire OS 5; the embedded browser matters for both the Companion app and kiosk apps.

Fire tablets with WebView 70 or newer and first-generation Chromecast devices remain above the new Chrome minimum. Yesterday’s formatting repairs did not change support requirements; these new minimums mean owners of permanently older displays need to check their browser version before upgrading.

pullRequests.title: Raise legacy browser floors to Chrome 67 and Safari/iOS 15

articles.title: Update Music Assistant before upgrading ESPHome Sendspin speakers
articles.dek: ESPHome 2026.10 requires Music Assistant 2.10.7 or 2.11.0b4 and newer for Sendspin connections.
body: ESPHome’s October release guidance tells owners of Sendspin speakers to update Music Assistant first. The encrypted protocol used by ESPHome 2026.10 requires Music Assistant 2.10.7 or 2.11.0b4 and newer; an older server will not connect to the updated device.

The expanded upgrade notes also flag configuration changes for makers: Sendspin requires ESP-IDF, artwork must use JPEG or PNG instead of BMP, and a media source’s codec list must include FLAC or PCM.

pullRequests.title: [sendspin] Cover the encrypted protocol and pairing in the 2026.10 release notes

externalSources.title: ESPHome 2026.10.0: Native ESP8266 builds and compressed updates

articles.title: Home Assistant hides setup choices that do not apply
articles.dek: Blueprints and integration forms can reveal settings as other choices change.
body: Home Assistant lets blueprint authors show only the inputs relevant to the choices someone has made. A fixed-brightness option, for example, can reveal its brightness field while other modes keep it out of the way. Whole sections can follow the same rule.

The same capability reaches integration setup and options forms. OpenAI Conversation uses it to put advanced settings beside its recommended-settings switch, hiding them while recommendations are enabled instead of adding a separate step.

Hidden form fields are neither required nor saved. Blueprint inputs still resolve to their configured default, or an empty value when they have none, so authors need to account for that when designing the automation.

pullRequests.title: Add conditional visibility to blueprint inputs
Add conditional inputs to blueprints
Add conditional field visibility to config and options flows
Hide OpenAI advanced options behind the recommended toggle

articles.title: Home Assistant’s installer prepares Wi-Fi before first boot
articles.dek: Supported computers receive their network settings as the installation image is written.
body: Home Assistant’s installer adds an optional Wi-Fi step after choosing the destination drive. Raspberry Pi 3, 4 and 5, Yellow with CM5, and generic x86-64 and aarch64 computers can receive their network name and password as the image is written.

The first boot imports the settings into the operating system’s network configuration and removes the temporary configuration from the boot partition. The extracted image on the computer stays unchanged. This setup supports password-protected WPA2 and mixed WPA2/WPA3 networks; open, hidden and WPA3-only networks are outside its scope.

pullRequests.title: Set up Wi-Fi while writing the image

articles.title: Matter.js Server repairs moves from the Python server
articles.dek: Failed migrations from version 1.5.0 require restoring a backup and trying again.
body: Matter.js Server corrects a migration failure that left devices unavailable with empty readings after moving from the Python Matter Server. Version 1.5.0 could create a new controller identity instead of using the identity the devices already trusted.

The migration now imports the existing identity into the storage the controller reads and refuses conflicting data instead of overwriting it. Installations already affected need to restore their migration backup and try again: automatically replacing the identity could cut off devices paired after the failed move. Importing further changes from the old server on later starts remains separate follow-up work.

pullRequests.title: fix(ws-controller): migrate the Python Matter Server CA into the storage the controller reads

articles.title: Home Assistant follows solar panels on a moving camper
articles.dek: Forecast.Solar can use changing location, direction and tilt without recreating its setup.
body: Home Assistant lets Forecast.Solar follow panels on a camper, caravan or other moving installation. The forecast can follow Home Assistant’s home location and take panel direction and tilt from sensors instead of requiring the integration to be removed and added again after moving.

Location changes refresh the forecast no more often than its update interval, protecting the service’s request allowance from continuous GPS updates. While running, an unreadable angle sensor keeps its last reading; after a restart or reload, forecasting waits until the required sensors have readings.

pullRequests.title: Update the forecast_solar integration to support sensor inputs

articles.title: Home Assistant combines household calendars into one
articles.dek: A calendar group follows events across work, school and family calendars.
body: Home Assistant adds calendar groups that combine several calendars into one read-only calendar. Work, school and family events can share a single entity, configured through the interface with a preview or through YAML.

The group shows the current event or the next one across its members and reports active while any member has an event under way. Nested groups use each underlying calendar once. Events still have to be created, edited or deleted in their original calendars.

pullRequests.title: Add support for calendar groups

articles.title: ESPHome runs small programs while the main processor sleeps
articles.dek: An ESP32 coprocessor keeps its state and can wake the main chip when needed.
body: ESPHome adds a way for makers to run a small C program on an ESP32’s low-power coprocessor while the main processor is in deep sleep. The program can run on a timer, share values with ESPHome and wake the main processor without losing its state.

The component supports the low-power RISC-V cores in ESP32-S2, S3, C5, C6 and P4 chips with native ESP-IDF builds. Tests on S3 and P4 boards kept a counter running across sleep and woke the main processor. P4 still needs a direct sleep call because ESPHome’s ordinary deep-sleep component does not yet compile there; the original ESP32 is outside this support.

pullRequests.title: [esp32_ulp][esp32] Add component to run programs on the ULP coprocessor
[esp32_ulp] Add ESP32 ULP coprocessor component documentation

articles.title: Home Assistant retires some UniFi Protect setup and health readings
articles.dek: A move away from the private interface removes several controls and diagnostics in 2027.1.
body: Home Assistant marks a set of UniFi Protect setup controls and health readings for removal in 2027.1. The integration is moving away from the private interface that supplies them, and UniFi’s official interface does not provide replacements.

The affected set includes SSH controls, analytics and insights switches, device uptime, wired link speed, recorder CPU and memory readings, and camera storage and data-rate readings. New installations and newly added devices no longer receive these entities; existing setups have the deprecation period to revise dashboards and automations.
Wi-Fi signal readings and the recorder’s storage and disk sensors remain. The removal concerns this specified group of settings and diagnostics, rather than camera viewing as a whole.

pullRequests.title: Deprecate the UniFi Protect device setup and health entities on the private API
Remove the deprecated UniFi Protect device setup and health entities

articles.title: Music Assistant’s AirPlay tool supports larger speaker groups
articles.dek: Nine or more AirPlay 2 receivers can share timing, and ended streams stop exhausting the service’s capacity.
body: Music Assistant’s AirPlay tool raises the limit of its shared timing service from eight receivers to 64. Groups of nine or more AirPlay 2 receivers could previously fail to start, while cycling through eight distinct receivers could leave later ones without the timing messages needed to play.

Marvin Schenkel also makes the service release a receiver’s place when its stream ends or its process disappears. Tests cover nine simultaneous receivers and reclaiming capacity after streams stop. The 64-receiver limit belongs to the timing service, rather than a guarantee of playback performance for a group that size.

pullRequests.title: Serve sync groups of any size and drop receivers of killed streams from the PTP daemon

articles.title: ESPHome corrects humidity readings from warm sensor enclosures
articles.dek: A new filter accounts for the temperature error that a fixed humidity offset cannot fix.
body: ESPHome adds a relative-humidity correction for sensors warmed by the electronics around them. Correcting the temperature alone leaves the humidity reading wrong, because relative humidity changes with temperature rather than by a fixed percentage offset.

The filter uses the corrected temperature and its configured offset to recalculate humidity, keeping the result between zero and 100 percent. It supports Celsius and Fahrenheit readings; temperatures outside minus 40 to 50 degrees Celsius pass through unchanged with a warning.

pullRequests.title: [sensor] Add Relative Humidity Correction Filter
[sensor] Add Relative Humidity Correction Filter

articles.title: Sendspin tightens the rules for pairing and permitted playback
articles.dek: The protocol closes two gaps that device and server implementations must address.
body: Sendspin’s protocol specification requires devices to reject audio and volume commands for playback roles they have not approved. Previously, the rules told a server not to send those messages without also requiring the receiver to ignore them.

A related pairing correction requires a fresh code entry for every attempt and limits the server to twenty rounds. Previously, only the client had that limit, leaving an intermediary a route to repeatedly guess against one entered code. These are requirements for device and server implementations; the specification changes alone do not establish protection in every Sendspin product.

pullRequests.title: Make clients ignore server messages for inactive roles
Bound dynamic pairing rounds on the server side

articles.title: Home Assistant connects LoRaWAN devices through two more networks
articles.dek: The Things Network and ChirpStack join the shared long-range device connection.
body: Home Assistant adds The Things Network and ChirpStack as connections for its shared LoRaWAN device support. Owners can select the applications supplying their devices, extending the long-range wireless system beyond the overview and SenseCAP readings covered earlier this week.

The Things Network setup offers region presets and custom servers; ChirpStack connects selected tenants and applications. These are new network connections for supported device integrations, rather than support for every device on either network.

Add ChirpStack integration
Document ChirpStack integration

articles.title: Home Assistant keeps sign-in secrets out of connection logs
articles.dek: Debug logging masks access tokens and passwords inside received messages.
body: Home Assistant stops writing sign-in tokens and account passwords into its WebSocket debug log. With that specific debug logging enabled, incoming authentication messages and account-management commands previously appeared unchanged.

Josef Zweck adds redaction to both received-message logging paths, including nested data and batches of messages. Current passwords, replacement passwords and client secrets join the fields that are hidden.

pullRequests.title: Redact secrets from received websocket messages in the debug log

articles.title: Home Assistant keeps dashboard controls in step with a device
articles.dek: Controls and readings follow the device without maintaining a manual list.
body: Home Assistant adds dashboard sections that follow one device’s entities as they are added or removed. The section can show tiles or a list, choose categories such as controls and sensors, and optionally display its area and battery level in the heading.

Hidden entities stay out, and individual entities can be excluded. Creating the section currently requires YAML; its visual editor can adjust it afterward, but adding it directly from the dashboard editor is separate follow-up work.

pullRequests.title: Add device section strategy

articles.title: Music Assistant keeps sound-based recommendations personal
articles.dek: One person’s recent listening stops appearing in another person’s discovery row.
body: Music Assistant keeps Sonic Similarity’s “Inspired by recently played” row separate for each user. It previously reused one person’s recommendations for everyone for up to a minute, including tracks from sources that other users were not allowed to see.
Marvin Schenkel makes the cached row follow the requesting account. AudioMuse-AI already kept this row separate; the correction brings Sonic Similarity into line.

pullRequests.title: Keep Sonic Similarity's "Inspired by recently played" row separate per user

articles.title: Community Day’s poster maker handles Chinese and Japanese text
articles.dek: Added character coverage and line wrapping help organizers create local event materials.
body: Community Day organizers can create event graphics containing common Chinese and Japanese characters with the Open Home Foundation’s asset generator. The change supplies the missing characters and wraps mixed text so a run of Chinese or Japanese writing does not behave like one unbreakable word.
Darren Griffin adds support for common simplified and traditional Chinese characters and Japanese kana. Rarer characters outside the included font subset can still appear as boxes.

pullRequests.title: Add Noto Sans SC font support for CJK text rendering

roadmapUpdates.title: Replacing automation steps moves into building
roadmapUpdates.summary: Niels’s proposal to replace an automation step while keeping compatible settings has moved from Approved to Building. The change advances development of the visual editor’s replacement controls; it does not establish their release.

sources.title: Let people change their mind about an automation step without rebuilding it

roadmapUpdates.title: Safer migration into app testing channels
roadmapUpdates.summary: Home Assistant is shaping how existing apps could move into shared stable, beta and development channels. After Wendelin proposed backup-based migration, Stefan Agner outlined a staged approach: early adopters first, then migration support for larger apps one by one.

sources.title: Per-App channels (stable/beta/dev) — share /data across pre-release variants
